name: Mascara / waterproof mascara
lead: Mascara is a cosmetic applied to the eyelashes to darken, thicken, lengthen and define them. It is most commonly a liquid in a tube with a brush applicator, and formulas are built from pigments, oils, waxes and preservatives. Waterproof versions use hydrophobic ingredients so they resist water and sweat.[1][2]

Eye darkening with kohl dates to about 4000 BC in ancient Egypt, and commercial mascara developed from the 19th-century work of Eugene Rimmel and the early 20th-century Maybelline business.[1] In looksmaxxing communities, some male users discuss mascara as a way to make the eye area look more defined, usually with concern about being noticed.[3]

Reported risks include allergic reactions, styes and eyelid swelling; waterproof products had the highest rate of detected organic fluorine, an indicator of PFAS, in a 2021 survey of cosmetics.[1] No clinical trials of mascara as a looks intervention were found.
infobox: Liquid, cream, powder; waterproof and non-waterproof

paras: Mascara coats lash hairs with pigment and conditioning ingredients to make them appear darker and fuller, and the effect is temporary. Water-resistant mascaras use hydrophobic ingredients such as dodecane, while non-waterproof versions use water-soluble bases.[1] Waterproof formulas were developed because earlier products ran with water or sweat.[1]

Kohl was used in ancient Egypt to darken lashes, lids and brows.[1][2] In the 19th century the French-born perfumer Eugene Rimmel developed a petroleum jelly-based product, and his name became a generic word for mascara in several languages.[1] Thomas Lyle Williams made a similar product for his sister Mabel in 1915-1917 and started a mail-order business in 1917 that became Maybelline.[1] Helene Winterstein-Kambersky patented a waterproof creme mascara in 1935, and Helena Rubinstein introduced a tube-and-brush product in 1957 and a refillable tube in 1958.[1]

Wikipedia reports that styes and swollen eyelids from allergic reactions are more common than toxic effects, with methylparaben, aluminum powder and benzyl alcohol among reported triggers. Mascara can also incubate microbes, and shelf life is stated as two to four months.[1] A review of contact dermatitis to cosmetics covers allergic reactions to cosmetic ingredients generally.[4]

The 1933 Lash Lure product, which contained para-phenylenediamine, was followed by blindness in several women and one death from infection; the US gave the FDA authority over cosmetics in 1938.[1] Kohl-type products such as kajal and surma often carry a lead poisoning risk and are described as illegal color additives in the United States.[1]

A 2021 study of 231 makeup and personal care products found organic fluorine, an indicator of PFAS, in over half; waterproof mascara had the highest rate, at 82 percent of brands tested.[1] A study of 100 Latina adolescents found that daily makeup users had higher urinary levels of some phthalates, parabens and phenols than rare users, though that study was not specific to mascara.[5]

On looksmax.org, some users post about trying mascara on the lower lashes or the eye area to make the eyes look more defined, and describe difficulty removing waterproof formulas without oil.[3] Other threads show users asking whether they look good wearing it.[6] Wikipedia's mascara article does not cover male use and refers readers to a separate page on male cosmetics.[1]

No studies found of mascara as an appearance intervention. Related research includes cosmetics-safety work such as the PFAS survey and the urinary biomarker study noted above, and a 2020 laboratory formulation study of a curling mascara with a thermoresponsive polymer.[1][5][7]

lore.intro: Mascara appears in looksmaxxing discussion as a low-cost way to define the eye area, with users commenting on the visibility of the result and on whether it is socially noticeable.[3]

claims.claim: Mascara on the lower lashes makes the eye area look more defined
claims.believers: One looksmax.org poster says darkening the lash lines made the eye area look better, with the lower lashes making the biggest difference, and that the main problem was avoiding being noticed.[3]
claims.experts: No published studies have examined mascara's effect on attractiveness in men. Reference sources describe its purpose as darkening, thickening and defining lashes.[1]

claims.claim: Waterproof mascara is hard to remove without oil
claims.believers: A poster reports that a waterproof product needed oil such as coconut oil to remove and took several minutes.[3]
claims.experts: Waterproof formulas use hydrophobic ingredients that resist water, which is consistent with the report.[1]

card.summary: A lash-darkening cosmetic with a long history; waterproof versions resist water and are harder to remove, and no research tests its looks effect.
card.note: Waterproof types ranked highest for detected organic fluorine (PFAS indicator) in a 2021 cosmetics survey.

quick.overview:
Mascara darkens, thickens and lengthens eyelashes using pigments, oils and waxes. Waterproof versions resist water and sweat and typically need an oil-based remover.

Some men in looksmaxxing forums discuss using it on the lower lashes for a more defined eye area. No clinical studies of its effect on attractiveness were found.
quick.mechanism: A pigmented coating on the lash hairs makes them look darker, thicker and longer; the effect is temporary and wears off or is washed away.
quick.risks: Reported problems include allergic reactions, eyelid swelling, styes and microbial contamination of old product. A 2021 study found organic fluorine, a PFAS marker, most often in waterproof mascara.
